## Introduction

This vignette demonstrates how to use Tidyverse functions to explore vehicle fuel efficiency.

The dataset is `mpg`, included in the `ggplot2` package. It contains vehicle fuel economy information originally collected by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.

I will use `dplyr` to clean and summarize the data and `ggplot2` to create visualizations.

The dataset contains 234 vehicle configurations from the 1999 and 2008 model years. The original `mpg` data remains unchanged; only the display names in the analysis tables are standardized.

## Load Packages and Data

```{r load-data}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)
library(stringr)

# Load the original vehicle fuel economy dataset.
# Keep the original mpg data unchanged for reproducibility.
data("mpg", package = "ggplot2")

# Standardize display names in tables and charts.
# This does not change the original dataset or numerical values.
format_vehicle_names <- function(data) {
  data %>%
    mutate(
      manufacturer = str_to_title(manufacturer),
      model = str_to_title(model),
      model = str_replace_all(model, regex("\\b4wd\\b", ignore_case = TRUE), "4WD"),
      model = str_replace_all(model, regex("\\bawd\\b", ignore_case = TRUE), "AWD"),
      class = recode(
        class,
        "2seater" = "Two Seater",
        "compact" = "Compact",
        "midsize" = "Mid-Size",
        "minivan" = "Minivan",
        "pickup" = "Pickup",
        "subcompact" = "Subcompact",
        "suv" = "SUV"
      )
    )
}

# Show the number of rows and columns

# Display dataset dimensions in a clear table
dataset_summary <- data.frame(
  Description = c(
    "Total Vehicle Records",
    "Total Variables"
  ),
  Value = c(
    nrow(mpg),
    ncol(mpg)
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  dataset_summary,
  col.names = c("Dataset Information", "Count"),
  caption = "Vehicle Fuel Economy Dataset Summary",
  row.names = FALSE
)

# Display the first six records

# Show a reader-friendly preview without changing mpg.
mpg_preview <- mpg %>% format_vehicle_names()

knitr::kable(
  head(mpg_preview, 6),
  col.names = c(
    "Manufacturer",
    "Vehicle Model",
    "Engine Size (L)",
    "Model Year",
    "Cylinders",
    "Transmission",
    "Drive Type",
    "City MPG",
    "Highway MPG",
    "Fuel Type",
    "Vehicle Class"
  ),
  caption = "Vehicle Fuel Economy Dataset",
  row.names = FALSE
)

```

## Data Cleaning and Transformation

The main variables are **Manufacturer**, **Vehicle Model**, **Model Year**, **Cylinders**, **City MPG**, **Highway MPG**, and **Vehicle Class**. MPG means *miles per gallon*, not miles per hour. The original variable names used in R (`cty`, `hwy`, `cyl`, and `class`) are retained so the analysis code remains reproducible.

In this section, I use `dplyr` functions to select, filter, and transform vehicle fuel economy data.

The functions demonstrated are `select()`, `filter()`, `mutate()`, and `arrange()`.

### Select Variables

The `select()` function keeps only the variables needed for the analysis. I also standardize manufacturer, model, and vehicle-class names once, so all later tables and charts use the same labels.

```{r select-variables}
vehicles <- mpg %>%
  select(manufacturer, model, year, cyl, cty, hwy, class) %>%
  format_vehicle_names()

knitr::kable(
  head(vehicles, 10),
  col.names = c(
    "Manufacturer", "Vehicle Model", "Model Year",
    "Cylinders", "City MPG", "Highway MPG",
    "Vehicle Class"
  ),
  caption = "Selected Vehicle Variables",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

### Filter Vehicles

The `filter()` function selects rows that meet a specific condition.

Here, I select vehicles with highway fuel efficiency of at least 30 miles per gallon.

```{r filter-vehicles}
efficient_vehicles <- vehicles %>%
  filter(hwy >= 30) %>%
  arrange(desc(hwy))

knitr::kable(
  head(efficient_vehicles, 10),
  col.names = c(
    "Manufacturer", "Vehicle Model", "Model Year",
    "Cylinders", "City MPG", "Highway MPG",
    "Vehicle Class"
  ),
  caption = "Vehicles with Highway MPG of at Least 30",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

### Create a New Variable

The `mutate()` function creates a new variable.

I calculate the difference between highway and city fuel efficiency.

```{r mutate-vehicles}
vehicles_clean <- vehicles %>%
  mutate(mpg_difference = hwy - cty) %>%
  arrange(desc(mpg_difference))

knitr::kable(
  head(vehicles_clean, 10),
  col.names = c(
    "Manufacturer",
    "Vehicle Model",
    "Model Year",
    "Cylinders",
    "City MPG",
    "Highway MPG",
    "Vehicle Class",
    "MPG Difference"
  ),
  caption = "Highway and City Fuel Efficiency Difference",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```


### Interpretation

I used `select()` to keep the most useful variables and `filter()` to identify vehicles with higher highway fuel efficiency.

I also used `mutate()` to calculate the difference between highway and city MPG. Vehicle classes and manufacturer names are displayed consistently throughout the vignette. Finally, `arrange()` helped organize the results.

These steps demonstrate how Tidyverse functions can prepare data for analysis.


## Data Summary

In this section, I use `dplyr` to summarize vehicle fuel efficiency by vehicle class.

The functions demonstrated are `group_by()`, `summarise()`, and `arrange()`.

### Average Fuel Efficiency by Vehicle Class

The `group_by()` function groups vehicles by class. The `summarise()` function calculates the average city and highway MPG for each group.

```{r summary-by-class}
fuel_summary <- vehicles_clean %>%
  group_by(class) %>%
  summarise(
    number_of_vehicles = n(),
    average_city_mpg = round(mean(cty, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    average_highway_mpg = round(mean(hwy, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(average_highway_mpg))

knitr::kable(
  fuel_summary,
  col.names = c(
    "Vehicle Class",
    "Number of Vehicles",
    "Average City MPG",
    "Average Highway MPG"
  ),
  caption = "Average Fuel Efficiency by Vehicle Class",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

### Identify the Most Fuel-Efficient Vehicle Classes

The `slice_head()` function selects the first three rows after sorting the results.

```{r most-efficient-classes}
top_classes <- fuel_summary %>%
  slice_head(n = 3)

knitr::kable(
  top_classes,
  col.names = c(
    "Vehicle Class",
    "Number of Vehicles",
    "Average City MPG",
    "Average Highway MPG"
  ),
  caption = "Three Most Fuel-Efficient Vehicle Classes",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

### Interpretation

The summary compares average fuel efficiency across different vehicle classes.

The vehicle classes with higher average highway MPG are more fuel-efficient on the highway.

This analysis demonstrates how `group_by()`, `summarise()`, and `arrange()` can be used to organize and compare data.


## Data Visualization

In this section, I use the `ggplot2` package to visualize vehicle fuel efficiency. These charts help compare highway and city MPG across different vehicle classes.

### Average Highway MPG by Vehicle Class

The `ggplot()` function creates a chart, while `geom_col()` displays the average highway MPG for each vehicle class. Each bar has its own color and a value label.

```{r highway-mpg-chart}
ggplot(
  fuel_summary,
  aes(
    x = reorder(class, average_highway_mpg),
    y = average_highway_mpg,
    fill = class
  )
) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +

  # Show MPG values next to each bar
  geom_text(
    aes(label = sprintf("%.1f MPG", average_highway_mpg)),
    hjust = -0.15,
    size = 3.8,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +

  coord_flip() +

  # Add space for the MPG labels
  scale_y_continuous(
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.22))
  ) +

  # Use different colors for vehicle classes
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +

  labs(
    title = "Average Highway Fuel Efficiency",
    subtitle = "Comparison by Vehicle Class",
    x = "Vehicle Class",
    y = "Average Highway MPG",
    caption = "Source: ggplot2 mpg dataset (EPA fuel economy data)"
  ) +

  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11),
    axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "none"
  )
```

### City MPG vs. Highway MPG

The `geom_point()` function creates a scatter plot to compare city and highway MPG for each vehicle configuration. Colors represent the vehicle class.


```{r city-highway-chart}
ggplot(
  vehicles_clean,
  aes(
    x = cty,
    y = hwy,
    color = class
  )
) +
  geom_point(
    size = 2.8,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(
    title = "City vs. Highway Fuel Efficiency",
    subtitle = "Comparison by Vehicle Class",
    x = "City Fuel Efficiency (MPG)",
    y = "Highway Fuel Efficiency (MPG)",
    color = "Vehicle Class",
    caption = "Source: ggplot2 mpg dataset"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 15
    ),
    legend.position = "right"
  )
```

### Interpretation

The first chart compares average highway fuel efficiency across vehicle classes. Classes with higher average MPG have better highway fuel efficiency.

The second chart shows the relationship between city and highway MPG. Vehicles with higher city MPG generally also have higher highway MPG.

These visualizations demonstrate how `ggplot2` helps identify patterns and compare numerical variables.

## Project Development Process

I developed this vignette using RStudio and Quarto.

First, I selected the `mpg` dataset from the `ggplot2` package. The dataset contains 234 vehicle records and 11 variables.

Next, I used `dplyr` to select important variables, filter vehicles, and calculate the difference between city and highway MPG.

I then used `group_by()` and `summarise()` to compare average fuel efficiency across vehicle classes.

After that, I created two visualizations using `ggplot2`. The first compares average highway MPG by vehicle class, and the second shows the relationship between city and highway MPG.

Finally, I reviewed the tables, labels, and results to make the example clear and easy to understand.

The code is organized step by step so classmates can reproduce the analysis and learn how to use Tidyverse functions.

## Results and Discussion

The dataset contains 234 vehicle records and 11 variables.

I used several Tidyverse functions to explore vehicle fuel efficiency.

- `select()` helped me choose the variables needed for analysis.
- `filter()` identified vehicles with at least 30 highway MPG.
- `mutate()` standardized display labels and created a variable to compare city and highway MPG.
- `group_by()` and `summarise()` calculated average fuel efficiency by vehicle class.
- `arrange()` organized the results.
- `ggplot()` created charts to visualize the data.

### Summary of Results

```{r final-summary}
# Calculate overall fuel efficiency
overall_summary <- vehicles_clean %>%
  summarise(
    total_vehicles = n(),
    average_city_mpg = round(mean(cty, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    average_highway_mpg = round(mean(hwy, na.rm = TRUE), 2)
  )

knitr::kable(
  overall_summary,
  col.names = c(
    "Total Vehicles",
    "Average City MPG",
    "Average Highway MPG"
  ),
  caption = "Overall Vehicle Fuel Efficiency Summary",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

### Discussion

The results show differences in fuel efficiency across vehicle classes.

The charts also show that vehicles with higher city MPG generally have higher highway MPG.

These results help explain how Tidyverse functions can be used to organize, summarize, and visualize a dataset.
